memoryText: And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness.
readingInstruction: Today there is no new reading. The week you have completed contained the binding of Isaac on Mount Moriah, one of the most theologically loaded chapters in the entire Old Testament. Take time today to let the depth of Abraham’s faith, and the foreshadowing of Christ’s sacrifice, settle in you.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Genesis 15:6 is the single most important Old Testament verse for understanding the New Testament’s doctrine of salvation. Paul quotes it in Romans 4 and Galatians 3 as the proof that justification has always been by faith, never by works.

Three things are happening here. Abraham believed, faith is the means, not earning. The LORD counted, the accounting is divine, not human. And what was counted was righteousness, not credit toward future righteousness, but righteousness itself.

Say the verse and notice: Abraham did nothing to earn this. He had lied about Sarai. He would lie again. He had not yet been circumcised. He had not yet faced Moriah. And he was reckoned righteous on the basis of believing. This is grace. This is also the verdict over you, if you have believed in Christ. Carry the verse with you as the legal verdict over your life. You are reckoned righteous, not because of who you are, but because of who Christ is.
weekInReview:
The week began with Abraham’s bold intercession for Sodom and the contrasting end of Lot’s compromised life. It moved through the long-awaited birth of Isaac, Sarah’s laughter, the fulfillment of twenty-five years of waiting. Then came Genesis 22, the binding of Isaac. The mountain of Moriah. The wood carried by the son. The ram caught in the thicket. The substitute provided by God. You worshiped with Psalm 105:23-45, which carried the patriarchal story forward into the Exodus. You watched Sarah die and Isaac receive Rebekah. And the week closed with the birth of Jacob and Esau, and the long pattern of the unloved younger son being chosen by God.

The week was about tested faith. Faith that lies sometimes. Faith that laughs in disbelief and then in fulfillment. Faith that climbs the mountain with the knife. Faith that, in spite of all its weakness, is reckoned as righteousness.
reflectionQuestions: What is your Isaac? Genesis 22 asks every believer this question eventually: what has God given you that you would struggle to give back to him? Name it today. Hold it loosely. The God who tested Abraham is the same God who did not spare his own Son. He has already given his most. Trust him with yours.

How does the binding of Isaac point you to the cross? Every detail of Genesis 22 anticipates Calvary, the beloved son carrying wood up the hill, the substitute provided by God, the son spared because another died. But at Moriah, the son was spared. At Calvary, the Son was not. Why does this matter? Sit with the difference today. How does the cross deepen your reading of Abraham’s near-sacrifice?

Where is your faith being tested right now, and what does Genesis 15:6 say to you in the test? Faith is not the absence of weakness. Abraham was reckoned righteous even with his lies still ahead of him. If you have believed in Christ, his righteousness has been reckoned to you, and that verdict holds even when your faith feels small.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that your standing with him is righteous in Christ, not good enough by your own effort.
Ask him to show you what you are holding too tightly and to help you hold it loosely.
Thank Jesus for carrying the wood and not being spared.
